{{otheruses||[[DIR EN GREY]]の[[ミュージック・ビデオ]]|鬼門 (映像作品)}} '''鬼門'''（きもん）とは、[[北東]]（[[艮]]＝うしとら：[[丑]]と[[寅]]の間）の[[方位]]・[[方位|方角]]のこと。日本では古来より鬼の出入り方角であるとして忌むべき方角とされる。 ==概説== 鬼門とは反対の[[南西]]（[[坤]]・[[未申]]）の方角を'''裏鬼門'''（うらきもん）と言い、この方角も鬼門同様、忌み嫌われる。北東（[[艮]]）を「鬼門」、南東（[[巽]]）を「風門・地門」、南西の裏鬼門を（人門・病門）、北西を（天門）とし、それぞれの四隅の方位・方角の[[陰陽道]]上の門の名である{{Sfn|日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|2015|p=37}}。『[[今昔物語集]]』にて[[陰陽師]]の[[弓削是雄]]が伴宿禰世継の自宅の艮の方向に暗殺者がいる事を予言した話などに[[艮]]を凶運と捉える観念がみられる<ref>{{cite book |last= 村山|first=修一 |author-link= 村山修一|date= |title=日本陰陽道史話 |url= |location= 東京|publisher= 平凡社|page=101|isbn=4-582-76406-1}}</ref>。[[台湾]]では鬼門は「この世とあの世をつなぐ」とされ[[7月 (旧暦)|旧暦7月]]（鬼月）に鬼門が開くといわれる<ref>{{cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれる旧暦7月の意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY(中華民国（台湾）外交部)|date=2016-08-12|accessdate=2020-08-22}}</ref>。
== 鬼門を恐れた理由 == 「鬼門」という言葉は、後漢の時代、[[王充]]『[[論衡]]（ろんこう）』訂鬼篇にひく「[[山海経]]」に見られる。{{Sfn|水野|2016|p=28-29}}
{{Quotation|「山海経」によれば、滄海（東海）のなかに度朔山（どさくさん）があり、山上には大桃木がある。三千里にもわたって曲がりくねり、枝の間の東北方を鬼門といい、そこは萬鬼（ばんき）が出入りするところとなっている。山上には二神人がいて（中略）、萬鬼をみはっていた。悪害をもたらす鬼は葦の縄で縛ってとらえ、虎の餌食とした。そこで黄帝は礼をつくり、時をみはからって、桃の木でつくった大きな人形を門に立て、門戸に二神人と虎を描いた絵を祀り、葦の縄をかけて凶魅（きょうみ）を防いだ。（ただし、現存する「山海経」にはこの記述はない）|}}
中国では年末年始は一年の変わり目の時期であり、冬から春に転じる時で変化が大きく、疫鬼（えきき）が民に病や災禍をもたらすとされた。そこで疫鬼を駆逐し、古い年を送り、新たな年、春の陽気、吉福を内に迎えた（「後漢書」礼儀志中に記載）。この歳事が日本に伝播し、次第に正月から立春前の節分の行事となったが、元々は旧暦の年越しの頃に厄払いとして行われた行事である。{{Sfn|水野|2016|p=31-32}}
一方、中国で古代から使われている[[十二支]]や[[式占|式盤]]では、季節と方位は連関している。つまり、一年の境界である大晦日は丑寅間にあたり、丑寅間は東北の方角にあたる。鬼が出現する大晦日＝丑寅間＝東北＝鬼の出現する門、鬼門となった。{{Sfn|水野|2016|p=163-164}}
東北鬼門の考え方は中国から伝播したものの、日本独自に発展している{{Sfn|水野|2016|p=164}}。陰陽道が日本に伝わり[[日本]]の[[神仏習合]]思想{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=11}}{{sfn|林淳|2005|p=52}} と深く関わりをもつことで、日本独自の[[家相]]の発展とともに鬼門の観念も発展してきた{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=36}}。
陰陽道の最盛期といわれる[[平安時代]]中期頃から、病気や疾病、地震、火災、天災など、そのすべてを[[神]]の[[祟り]]が起こすものと考えられ、祟りを起こす[[神]]の存在を[[鬼]]に例えて恐れたことが大きな理由とされる{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=36}}{{sfn|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{sfn|繁田信一|2006|p=129}}。鎌倉時代前期に著された「陰陽道旧記抄」に「竈、門、井、厠、者家神也云々」とあり、竈、門、井戸、厠など、病気に直結する場所を[[神格化]]させ、諸々の[[宅神]]から祟りをうけぬよう[[祭祀]]を行っていた歴史があり、[[鬼]]の門と名の付く北東方位を他の方位方角より恐れる方位になった{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=36}}{{sfn|林淳|2005|p=52,53}}。
== 鬼門の捉え方（権力者） == 時の統制者は、京内を結界（聖と俗を分離）し、人々が暮らす京内に災い事が起きないよう四角四境の祭祀を行っていた。代表的なものに、京城四隅疫神祭（都）、宮城四隅疫神祭（内裏）があり、四方を平等に崇めていた{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=37}}{{sfn|林淳|2005|p=53}}{{sfn|繁田信一|2006|p=72,74,75,76}}{{sfn|林淳|2005|p=75,76,77}}{{sfn|岡田荘司|2010|p=136,137}} 歴史がある。現在でも地鎮祭で四方を囲み結界をつくり、その土地に災いが起きぬよう祭礼を行う地鎮祭が引き継がれており、同じく四方を平等に崇めている{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=36}}。また、歴代天皇は、正月元旦、早朝から四方を拝され、年災消滅、五穀豊穣を祈る[[四方拝]]といわれる[[祭祀]]を行っていて、それは寛平二年（890）から現在の天皇まで1100年以上続いている{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=37}}{{sfn|林淳|2005|p=53}}。
鎌倉時代初期の僧[[慈円]]は、[[比叡山]]が、都の[[丑寅]]の方角にある鬼の門を塞いでいると[[和歌]]に詠んだ<ref>{{cite book |last= 村山|first=修一 |author-link= 村山修一|date= |title=日本陰陽道史話 |url= |location= 東京|publisher= 平凡社|page=128 |isbn=4-582-76406-1}}</ref>。
武家の世界では多くの城で鬼門方位に厠をつくることが常道とされていた<ref name="城の日本史">{{Cite book|和書|title=城の日本史|date=2011年8月|year=2011|publisher=講談社}}</ref>。[[安土城]]、[[福知山城]]、[[岡山城]]、[[姫路城]]などは裏鬼門に厠が配されていたとされ{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=20}}<ref name="城の日本史"/>、鬼神の災いを恐れず覚悟を持った[[武将]]の気構えと捉えることができる、と論じている{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=21}}。
江戸中期の学者[[新井白石]]は『鬼門説』を著し、当時一般的になっていた鬼門の観念について、その起源などの考察をおこなった<ref>{{Cite journal|和書|author=水野杏紀 |title= 新井白石『鬼門説』について : 翻刻と注解 (平木康平教授退職記念号) |journal=人文学論集. 平木康平教授退職記念号 |ISSN=0289-6192 |publisher=大阪府立大学人文学会 |year=2008 |month=mar |issue=26 |pages=97-117 |naid=110007145726 |doi=10.24729/00004460 |url=https://doi.org/10.24729/00004460 |access-date=2021-12-02}}</ref>。
== 鬼門の捉え方（庶民） ==
十二支で鬼門（丑寅）とは反対の方角が[[未申]]であることから、[[サル|猿]]の像を鬼門避けとして祀ったり、[[京都御所]]の北東角の軒下に木彫りの猿が鎮座し、築地塀がそこだけ凹んでおり、「[[猿ヶ辻]]」と称されてきた。
[[京都御所]]の[[築地塀]]が鬼門、北東方位を凹ませてつくられていることから、「御所が鬼門を避けている」「除けている」と考えられ、それが鬼門を除ける手法とされてきた。
東京芸術大学、東京工業大学名誉教授 清家清の著書 「現代の家相」{{Sfn|清家清|1989|p=46}}には、「家相の教え通りに凹ませている」と書かれている。現代でも人々は縁起を担ぎ、家の北東、鬼門の方角に魔よけの意味をもつ、[[ヒイラギ]]や[[ナンテン]]、[[オモト]]を植えたり、鬼門や[[裏鬼門]]（南西）から水回りや玄関を避けて家作りをする場合がある。京都のNPO法人が2015年、京都市内中心部だけで、ビルや店舗、一般住宅など、約1100か所に鬼門除けがあるという調査がなされ、四角く囲って玉砂利を敷いたり、ヒイラギ、南天を植えている調査結果が発表されている{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=28}}。
[[File:猿ヶ辻.jpg|thumb|京都御所の築地塀 北東角の部分]]
<!-- 出典はひとつだけでなく他にも鬼の間と鬼門の関連を指摘する出典をあげて下さい-->[[京都御所]]の内部には[[鬼の間]]が存在している。[[鬼の間]]とは、[[京都御所]]において[[仁寿殿]]の西、後涼殿の東にある[[清涼殿]]の南西隅の部屋であり、すなわち[[裏鬼門]]の位置にある。[[飛鳥部常則]]が[[康保]]元年（[[964年]]）に鬼を退治する[[白沢王]]像を描いたとされている。[[順徳天皇]]が著した『[[禁秘抄]]』にこれに関する記述がある。壁に描かれていた王は、一人で剣をあげて鬼を追う勇姿であり、それを白沢王といい、古代インド波羅奈国（はらなこく）の王であり、鬼を捕らえた剛勇の武将であると言う説がある。 現在の建物（鬼の間）に、白澤王の絵は描かれていない{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=31}}。なお、江戸中期の随筆「夏山雑談」には、白沢王は李将軍、「白澤王」としても記されている{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=31}}。京都御所、天皇家が鬼の災い、神の祟り（自然災害、火災、疫病の蔓延）を恐れて、築地塀を凹ませていた、という解釈より、庶民に災いごとがふりかからないように、皇室が一手に凹みで受けとめて、御所内部の[[清涼殿]]、[[鬼の間]]に導いて鬼を切り倒し、世の安泰を願っていた、そう解釈したほうが自然であると、家相を研究する小池康寿は著書で{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=31}}論じる。現代でも皇居の間取りは公開されておらず、外から見ただけの塀の凹みだけを受けて鬼門除けに繋がったと考えた方が理に適うとしている{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=32}}。[[猿ヶ辻]]に関しても前述とは別に御所を守護する[[日吉神社]]の神の使いが猿だったことから、「猿ヶ辻」と呼ばれる記述もある。昭和43年、[[皇居東御苑]]が一般公開されたが、[[京都御所]]は[[GHQ]]の管理下でありながら、昭和21年11月に一般公開されたが、現在でも[[鬼の間]]は一般公開されていない{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=31}}。
== 鬼門の否定 == [[明治維新]]・近代化によって鬼門は[[迷信]]とされるようになり、[[大正]]時代には[[京大]]総長・中国古代史研究者 [[新城新蔵]]が『迷信』を出版し、鬼門・方位・暦を一刀両断し、鬼門は「単なるこけおどし」と批判した{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=39}}<ref>『[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1021635/64 迷信]』第1章（4）「こけ威しの鬼門」p113-126（国立国会図書館）</ref>。一方で民衆間の信仰は続いた。[[井上円了]]によると、[[大正]]時代でも長野県の村では「学校の土地が鬼門に触れている」という理由で村会で議論になったといい、井上はそれを批判している<ref>[[井上円了]]『[https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/001021/files/49374_58731.html 迷信と宗教]』 ([[青空文庫]])</ref>。
[[文部省]]は[[内務省 (日本)|内務省]]とともに[[淫祠邪教]]による迷信を取り締まる立場であった。[[1936年]]（昭和11年）、[[松田源治]]、[[川崎卓吉]]と歴代文部大臣経験者が急逝した直後に、鬼門の位置に造ったばかりの大臣専用便所を取り壊した。大阪毎日新聞は、迷信を取り締まる立場の者が、とんでもない行為を行っているとして文部省を批判した<ref>文教当局と迷信、恥ずかしい話『大阪毎日新聞』昭和11年4月8日（『昭和ニュース事典第5巻 昭和10年-昭和11年』本編p712 昭和ニュース事典編纂委員会 毎日コミュニケーションズ刊 1994年）</ref>。
[[風水師]] [[リリアン・トゥー]]は鬼門である北東方位を「地獄の門」とすることに疑問があるとしている<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|和書|title=図説 風水大全|date=1998-9-10|publisher=東洋書林|pages=|author=リリアン・トゥー|page=129}}</ref>。
== 鬼門をなくす祭祀 出雲屋敷地鎮祭 == 本来は出雲の氏子のみを対象に行っていた祭祀。{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=187}}現在では、他県から訪れるものも、神殿において、地鎮祭の式典が行われ、新築や増築工事に対する地鎮祭が行われる。{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=187}}その地鎮祭を出雲屋敷地鎮祭という。{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=187}}式典後、土地に鎮める「御土」「鎮め物」、また中央、四方、五カ所の柱に貼る御札を頂き、それを五柱御札という。{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=187}}土地や建物の穢れをなくし、鬼門という考え方もいっさいなくなる祭祀となる。{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=187}}※神語三唱や御神土埋納、四拍手など特殊性がある。出雲屋敷後、年々多少の初穂を献納する'''出雲年貢'''を行う地域がある<ref>『出雲大社教布教師養成講習会』発行出雲大社教教務本庁平成元年9月1日全218頁中230頁</ref>。
== 鬼門と寺院との関係 == [[平城京]]では鬼門の方向に[[東大寺]]（創建年8世紀前半）が、裏鬼門の方向に植槻八幡宮が、[[平安京]]では[[大内裏]]から鬼門の方向に[[比叡山延暦寺]]が、裏鬼門の方向に[[石清水八幡宮]]が、[[鎌倉]]では[[鎌倉幕府|幕府]]から鬼門の方向に[[荏柄天神社]]が、裏鬼門の方角に[[本覚寺 (鎌倉市)|夷堂]]が、[[江戸]]では[[江戸城]]から鬼門の方向に東叡山[[寛永寺]]が、裏鬼門の方向に三縁山広度院[[増上寺]]が置かれたといわれている。また平安京の表鬼門の方向には[[吉田神社]]があり、これとは別に[[赤山禅院]]は表鬼門で信仰を集めた<ref>{{Cite web|和書|title=京都の表鬼門を護る|url= http://www.sekizanzenin.com/kimon.html|accessdate=2021-06-14|website=天台宗 比叡山延暦寺 皇城表鬼門 赤山禅院}}</ref>。
[[神仏習合]]が大きく影響しており、[[伊勢神宮]]の丑寅（北東）に位置する[[金剛證寺]]（こんごうしょうじ）創建年（伝）6世紀 が「伊勢神宮の鬼門を守る寺」として[[伊勢信仰]]と結びつき、「伊勢へ参らば朝熊をかけよ、朝熊かけねば[[片参り]]」{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=99}}とされ、[[伊勢国|伊勢]]・[[志摩国|志摩]]最大の寺となった。[[虚空蔵菩薩]]の眷属、[[雨宝童子]]が祀られており、当時は[[天照大御神]]の[[化現]]と考えられたため、[[伊勢皇大神宮]]の奥の院とされた。{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=100}}それらから、仏事に用いられる[[樒]]（しきみ）ではなく、神事に使われる[[榊]]（さかき）が供えられる、全国でも珍しい寺である{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=100}}。しかし、伊勢神宮を代表するようにすべて神仏習合時代に後付けで言われた、つくられたものである{{Sfn|小池|2015|p=100}}。
== 俗語の「鬼門」 == 以上のように、鬼門は本来呪術的な意味を持つ言葉であるが、転じて「よくない結果が起こりやすい事柄」に対してこの言葉が用いられるようになっていった（例<ref>{{Cite news|date=2021-03-16|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXZQOFK133AH0T10C21A3000000/|title=みずほ障害、重い4度目 鬼門のバッチ処理でつまずき|newspaper=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2022-03-05}}</ref>）。
方角に限らず、場所、[[時間帯]]や特定の教科などを指すこともあったり、[[放送]]業界（[[テレビ]]・[[ラジオ]]）でも[[打ち切り]]が複数の番組で連続して続く放送枠に対して用いられていたりする為、その用途は幅広い。ミュージシャンの[[大瀧詠一]]は生前、アルバムの発売日を誕生日に据えるとコンセプト変更で製作延長等発売延期になる為に誕生日を鬼門としていた。

[[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:Kk]][[en:Kimon]][[en:Kimon]][[ja:鬼門]] [[en:Kimon (鬼門)]] '''Kōfu''' (会符) refers to a shipping tag used during the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代}} by the {{ill|Imperial Court of Japan|ja|朝廷 (日本)}} (Imperial Court), the {{ill|Tokugawa shogunate|ja|江戸幕府}} (shogunate), {{ill|kuge|ja|公家}} (court nobles), {{ill|buke|ja|武家}} (samurai families), and {{ill|temples and shrines|ja|寺社}} to indicate the ownership of transported goods. It was also known as '''Kōrifu''' (行李符), '''Efu''' (絵符), or '''Denfu''' (伝符).
== Description == For the {{ill|Imperial Court of Japan|ja|朝廷 (日本)}} and the {{ill|Tokugawa shogunate|ja|江戸幕府}}, the tags were marked simply with "{{ill|Goyō|ja|御用}}" alongside the {{ill|Chrysanthemum Seal|ja|菊花紋章}} or {{ill|Triple Hollyhock|ja|三つ葉葵}} crests. In other cases, the tags would indicate the specific affiliation, such as "○○ {{ill|Goyō|ja|御用}}" or "×× {{ill|Household|ja|家中}} ÷÷ {{ill|Goyō|ja|御用}}," accompanied by family crests.
Goods bearing a {{ill|Kōfu|ja|会符}} tag were granted special privileges, allowing transportation at the government-regulated '''{{ill|Osadame Chinsen|ja|御定賃銭}}''' rates when utilizing {{ill|post stations|ja|宿場}} and {{ill|relay horses|ja|伝馬}}. Notably, goods designated for the {{ill|Tokugawa family|ja|徳川将軍家}} (shōgun's household goods) were mandated to be transported free of charge.
== Issues in the 18th Century == From the mid-18th century, as {{ill|commercial distribution|ja|商品流通}} flourished, the disparity between the government-regulated {{ill|Osadame Chinsen|ja|御定賃銭}} and the market-based '''{{ill|Aitai Chinsen|ja|相対賃銭}}''' grew. Consequently, {{ill|nobles|ja|公家}}, {{ill|samurai|ja|武家}}, and {{ill|temples and shrines|ja|寺社}} began leasing {{ill|Kōfu|ja|会符}} tags to {{ill|merchants|ja|商人}} and {{ill|farmers|ja|百姓}} for a fee, enabling them to benefit from the lower {{ill|Osadame Chinsen|ja|御定賃銭}} rates. Although the {{ill|Tokugawa shogunate|ja|江戸幕府}} frequently prohibited this practice, such bans proved ineffective.
== References == * Yukitaka Kodama, "{{ill|Kōfu|ja|会符}}" in ''{{ill|Kokushi Daijiten 2|ja|国史大辞典}}'' (Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 1980), ISBN 978-4-642-00502-9 * Yasunari Maruyama, "{{ill|Kōfu|ja|会符}}" in ''{{ill|Nihonshi Daijiten 1|ja|日本史大事典}}'' (Heibonsha, 1992), ISBN 978-4-582-13101-7
== Related Topics == * {{ill|History of Japanese Transportation|ja|日本の交通史}} * {{ill|Tokugawa Shogunate|ja|江戸幕府}} * {{ill|Japanese Feudal System|ja|日本の封建制度}}

[[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:Kk]][[en:Kimon]][[en:Kimon]][[ja:鬼門]] [[en:Kimon (鬼門)]] '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東}} direction ({{ill|艮|ja|艮}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西}} ({{ill|坤|ja|坤}}, representing {{ill|未|ja|未}} and {{ill|申|ja|申}}), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}}, the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the {{ill|Lunheng|ja|論衡}} by {{ill|Wang Chong|ja|王充}}, referencing the {{ill|Shan Hai Jing|ja|山海経}}. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}} saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山}} was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}. In {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}}, a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿}}) guards the northeast corner, known as {{ill|Sarugatsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻}}. People planted {{ill|holly|ja|ヒイラギ}} and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like {{ill|Arinori Mori|ja|森有礼}} criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.
== References == * Seikei Kiyoshi, ''Modern House Fortunes'' (1989), ISBN 978-4106019678 * Yasuhisa Koike, ''The Correct Home Fortunes for Japanese People'' (2015), ISBN 978-4833421492

== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未}} and {{ill|Monkey (zodiac)|ja|申}}), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}}, the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the {{ill|Lunheng|ja|論衡}} by {{ill|Wang Chong|ja|王充}}, referencing the {{ill|Shan Hai Jing|ja|山海経}}. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}} saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山}} was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}. In {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}}, a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿}}) guards the northeast corner, known as {{ill|Sarugatsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻}}. People planted {{ill|holly|ja|ヒイラギ}} and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like {{ill|Arinori Mori|ja|森有礼}} criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.
== References == * Seikei Kiyoshi, ''Modern House Fortunes'' (1989), ISBN 978-4106019678 * Yasuhisa Koike, ''The Correct Home Fortunes for Japanese People'' (2015), ISBN 978-4833421492
== Related Topics == * {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} * {{ill|Feng Shui|ja|風水}} * {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}} * {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮}}

[[Category:qq-Kimon-->[[Category:qq deprecated close]] [[Category:Kk]][[en:Kimon]][[en:Kimon]][[ja:鬼門]] [[en:Kimon (鬼門)]] '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東}} direction ({{ill|艮|ja|艮}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未}} and {{ill|Monkey (zodiac)|ja|申}}), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}}, the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the {{ill|Lunheng|ja|論衡}} by {{ill|Wang Chong|ja|王充}}, referencing the {{ill|Shan Hai Jing|ja|山海経}}. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}} saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山}} was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}. In {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}}, a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿}}) guards the northeast corner, known as {{ill|Sarugatsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻}}. People planted {{ill|holly|ja|ヒイラギ}} and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like {{ill|Arinori Mori|ja|森有礼}} criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.
== References == * Seikei Kiyoshi, ''Modern House Fortunes'' (1989), ISBN 978-4106019678 * Yasuhisa Koike, ''The Correct Home Fortunes for Japanese People'' (2015), ISBN 978-4833421492
== See Also == * {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} * {{ill|Feng Shui|ja|風水}} * {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}} * {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮}}

[[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq deprecated open]]<!--Kimon--> [[Category:Kk]][[en:Kimon]][[en:Kimon]][[ja:鬼門]] [[en:Kimon (鬼門)]] '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東}} direction ({{ill|艮|ja|艮}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未}} and {{ill|Monkey (zodiac)|ja|申}}), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}}, the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the {{ill|Lunheng|ja|論衡}} by {{ill|Wang Chong|ja|王充}}, referencing the {{ill|Shan Hai Jing|ja|山海経}}. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}} saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山}} was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}. In {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}}, a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿}}) guards the northeast corner, known as {{ill|Sarugatsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻}}. People planted {{ill|holly|ja|ヒイラギ}} and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like {{ill|Arinori Mori|ja|森有礼}} criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.

== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未}} and {{ill|Monkey (zodiac)|ja|申}}), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}}, the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門}} in the northwest.

For example, {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山}} was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}.

== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未}} and {{ill|Monkey (zodiac)|ja|申}}), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}}, the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the {{ill|Lunheng|ja|論衡}} by {{ill|Wang Chong|ja|王充}}, referencing the {{ill|Shan Hai Jing|ja|山海経}}. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}} saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山}} was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}}. In {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}}, a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿}}) guards the northeast corner, known as {{ill|Sarugatsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻}}. People planted {{ill|holly|ja|ヒイラギ}} and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like {{ill|Arinori Mori|ja|森有礼}} criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.

==Merged second translation== {{otheruses||[[:en:Dir En Grey|Dir En Grey]]'s [[:en:Music video|Music Video]]|鬼門 (映像作品)}} '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the northeastern direction ({{ill|Ushitora|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ushitora|qq=}}, "Ox and Tiger": between the {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}} on the Chinese zodiac). In Japan, this direction has traditionally been considered ominous and is associated with the entrance and exit of demons.
== Overview ==
The direction opposite to Kimon, the southwest ({{ill|Kon|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kon|qq=}}, {{ill|Hinoeuma|ja|未申|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoeuma|qq=}}), is called '''Urakimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded as inauspicious. Kimon (northeast) is associated with "demon gate," while the southwest (Urakimon) is referred to as "people gate" or "illness gate," the southeast ({{ill|Sun|ja|巽|1=Xun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=巽|lt=Xun (巽)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sun|qq=}}) as "wind gate," and the northwest as "heaven gate" according to [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|author=小池康寿|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> In the [[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatari]], an [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]] named {{ill|Yuge no Koreo|ja|弓削是雄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuge no Koreo|qq=}} predicts an assassin's presence in the northeast direction of {{ill|Tomonokimi Yotsugi|ja|伴宿禰世継|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tomonokimi Yotsugi|qq=}}’s residence, illustrating a perception of艮as an unlucky direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=101|ISBN=4-582-76406-1}}</ref> In {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taiwan|qq=}}, Kimon is considered the "gateway between this world and the next," opening during the {{ill|Ghost Month|ja|鬼月|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ghost Month|qq=}} in the seventh lunar month.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれるLunisolar Julyの意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY|date=2016-08-12}}</ref>
== Reasons for Fearing Kimon ==
The term "Kimon" appears in the Eastern Han period's [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]]’s ''[[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]]'', in the ''Correcting Ghosts'' chapter, citing the ''[[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Classic of Mountains and Seas]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=28-29}}</ref>
{{Quotation|According to the ''Classic of Mountains and Seas,'' there is a Dousaku Mountain (度朔山) in the Eastern Sea. Atop the mountain stands a giant peach tree that spans 3,000 ri, curving around its branches. The area between the branches to the northeast is called Kimon, where myriad ghosts pass through. Two divine figures guard this place, binding malevolent ghosts with reed ropes to be fed to tigers. Consequently, the Yellow Emperor established rituals, erecting a large peachwood doll at the gate and hanging reed ropes to ward off evil spirits.|}}
In ancient China, the transition from winter to spring marked the year’s end, a period associated with ghosts causing diseases and calamities. Rituals were performed to drive out these spirits and welcome spring’s fortune. These practices, transmitted to Japan, evolved into seasonal events like [[:en:Setsubun|Setsubun]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=31-32}}</ref>
Kimon's association with demons also stems from its connection to {{ill|Onmyōdō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōdō|qq=}} practices that integrated with Japan's [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|pages=36-37}}</ref>

== Popular Practices ==
Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.

==Merged second translation== {{otheruses||[[:en:Dir En Grey|Dir En Grey]]'s [[:en:Music video|Music Video]]|鬼門 (映像作品)}} '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the northeastern direction ({{ill|Ushitora|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ushitora|qq=}}, "Ox and Tiger": between the {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}} on the Chinese zodiac). In Japan, this direction has traditionally been considered ominous and is associated with the entrance and exit of demons.
== Overview ==
The direction opposite to Kimon, the southwest ({{ill|Kon|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kon|qq=}}, {{ill|Hinoeuma|ja|未申|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoeuma|qq=}}), is called '''Urakimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded as inauspicious. Kimon (northeast) is associated with "demon gate," while the southwest (Urakimon) is referred to as "people gate" or "illness gate," the southeast ({{ill|Sun|ja|巽|1=Xun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=巽|lt=Xun (巽)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sun|qq=}}) as "wind gate," and the northwest as "heaven gate" according to [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|author=小池康寿|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> In the [[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatari]], an [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]] named {{ill|Yuge no Koreo|ja|弓削是雄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuge no Koreo|qq=}} predicts an assassin's presence in the northeast direction of {{ill|Tomonokimi Yotsugi|ja|伴宿禰世継|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tomonokimi Yotsugi|qq=}}’s residence, illustrating a perception of艮as an unlucky direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=101|ISBN=4-582-76406-1}}</ref> In {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taiwan|qq=}}, Kimon is considered the "gateway between this world and the next," opening during the {{ill|Ghost Month|ja|鬼月|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ghost Month|qq=}} in the seventh lunar month.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれるLunisolar Julyの意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY|date=2016-08-12}}</ref>
== Reasons for Fearing Kimon ==
The term "Kimon" appears in the Eastern Han period's [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]]’s ''[[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]]'', in the ''Correcting Ghosts'' chapter, citing the ''[[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Classic of Mountains and Seas]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=28-29}}</ref>
{{Quotation|According to the ''Classic of Mountains and Seas,'' there is a Dousaku Mountain (度朔山) in the Eastern Sea. Atop the mountain stands a giant peach tree that spans 3,000 ri, curving around its branches. The area between the branches to the northeast is called Kimon, where myriad ghosts pass through. Two divine figures guard this place, binding malevolent ghosts with reed ropes to be fed to tigers. Consequently, the Yellow Emperor established rituals, erecting a large peachwood doll at the gate and hanging reed ropes to ward off evil spirits.|}}
In ancient China, the transition from winter to spring marked the year’s end, a period associated with ghosts causing diseases and calamities. Rituals were performed to drive out these spirits and welcome spring’s fortune. These practices, transmitted to Japan, evolved into seasonal events like [[:en:Setsubun|Setsubun]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=31-32}}</ref>
Kimon's association with demons also stems from its connection to {{ill|Onmyōdō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōdō|qq=}} practices that integrated with Japan's [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|pages=36-37}}</ref>
== Perceptions of Kimon (Authority) ==
Rulers established rituals like the Kyoto’s {{ill|Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|qq=}} to protect the city from disasters.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> For example, the monk [[:en:Jien|Jien]] described [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] as guarding Kyoto’s northeastern Kimon direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=128}}</ref>
== Popular Practices ==
Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

[[sn:Ura Kimon]] [[en:Ura Kimon]] [[ja:鬼門]]

[[Category:Merged pages]] [[Category:qq]]<!--Doing this to bump these pages because my history retrieval attempts have led to category caching errors-->[[sn:Kimon]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:方位]] [[Category:East Asian folk religion]]

'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.

'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.
== References == * Seikei Kiyoshi, ''Modern House Fortunes'' (1989), ISBN 978-4106019678 * Yasuhisa Koike, ''The Correct Home Fortunes for Japanese People'' (2015), ISBN 978-4833421492
== See Also == * [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] * [[:en:Feng shui|Feng Shui]] * [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] * [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]]

==Merged second translation== {{otheruses||[[:en:Dir En Grey|Dir En Grey]]'s [[:en:Music video|Music Video]]|鬼門 (映像作品)}} '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the northeastern direction ({{ill|Ushitora|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ushitora|qq=}}, "Ox and Tiger": between the {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}} on the Chinese zodiac). In Japan, this direction has traditionally been considered ominous and is associated with the entrance and exit of demons.
== Overview ==
The direction opposite to Kimon, the southwest ({{ill|Kon|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kon|qq=}}, {{ill|Hinoeuma|ja|未申|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoeuma|qq=}}), is called '''Urakimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded as inauspicious. Kimon (northeast) is associated with "demon gate," while the southwest (Urakimon) is referred to as "people gate" or "illness gate," the southeast ({{ill|Sun|ja|巽|1=Xun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=巽|lt=Xun (巽)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sun|qq=}}) as "wind gate," and the northwest as "heaven gate" according to [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|author=小池康寿|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> In the [[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatari]], an [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]] named {{ill|Yuge no Koreo|ja|弓削是雄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuge no Koreo|qq=}} predicts an assassin's presence in the northeast direction of {{ill|Tomonokimi Yotsugi|ja|伴宿禰世継|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tomonokimi Yotsugi|qq=}}’s residence, illustrating a perception of艮as an unlucky direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=101|ISBN=4-582-76406-1}}</ref> In {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taiwan|qq=}}, Kimon is considered the "gateway between this world and the next," opening during the {{ill|Ghost Month|ja|鬼月|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ghost Month|qq=}} in the seventh lunar month.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれるLunisolar Julyの意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY|date=2016-08-12}}</ref>
== Reasons for Fearing Kimon ==
The term "Kimon" appears in the Eastern Han period's [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]]’s ''[[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]]'', in the ''Correcting Ghosts'' chapter, citing the ''[[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Classic of Mountains and Seas]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=28-29}}</ref>
{{Quotation|According to the ''Classic of Mountains and Seas,'' there is a Dousaku Mountain (度朔山) in the Eastern Sea. Atop the mountain stands a giant peach tree that spans 3,000 ri, curving around its branches. The area between the branches to the northeast is called Kimon, where myriad ghosts pass through. Two divine figures guard this place, binding malevolent ghosts with reed ropes to be fed to tigers. Consequently, the Yellow Emperor established rituals, erecting a large peachwood doll at the gate and hanging reed ropes to ward off evil spirits.|}}
In ancient China, the transition from winter to spring marked the year’s end, a period associated with ghosts causing diseases and calamities. Rituals were performed to drive out these spirits and welcome spring’s fortune. These practices, transmitted to Japan, evolved into seasonal events like [[:en:Setsubun|Setsubun]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=31-32}}</ref>
Kimon's association with demons also stems from its connection to {{ill|Onmyōdō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōdō|qq=}} practices that integrated with Japan's [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|pages=36-37}}</ref>
== Perceptions of Kimon (Authority) ==
Rulers established rituals like the Kyoto’s {{ill|Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|qq=}} to protect the city from disasters.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> For example, the monk [[:en:Jien|Jien]] described [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] as guarding Kyoto’s northeastern Kimon direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=128}}</ref>
== Popular Practices ==
Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

revision.text:
'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.
== References == * Seikei Kiyoshi, ''Modern House Fortunes'' (1989), ISBN 978-4106019678 * Yasuhisa Koike, ''The Correct Home Fortunes for Japanese People'' (2015), ISBN 978-4833421492
== See Also == * [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] * [[:en:Feng shui|Feng Shui]] * [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] * [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]]

==Merged second translation== {{otheruses||[[:en:Dir En Grey|Dir En Grey]]'s [[:en:Music video|Music Video]]|鬼門 (映像作品)}} '''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the northeastern direction ({{ill|Ushitora|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ushitora|qq=}}, "Ox and Tiger": between the {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}} on the Chinese zodiac). In Japan, this direction has traditionally been considered ominous and is associated with the entrance and exit of demons.
== Overview ==
The direction opposite to Kimon, the southwest ({{ill|Kon|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kon|qq=}}, {{ill|Hinoeuma|ja|未申|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoeuma|qq=}}), is called '''Urakimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded as inauspicious. Kimon (northeast) is associated with "demon gate," while the southwest (Urakimon) is referred to as "people gate" or "illness gate," the southeast ({{ill|Sun|ja|巽|1=Xun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=巽|lt=Xun (巽)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sun|qq=}}) as "wind gate," and the northwest as "heaven gate" according to [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|author=小池康寿|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> In the [[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatari]], an [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]] named {{ill|Yuge no Koreo|ja|弓削是雄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuge no Koreo|qq=}} predicts an assassin's presence in the northeast direction of {{ill|Tomonokimi Yotsugi|ja|伴宿禰世継|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tomonokimi Yotsugi|qq=}}’s residence, illustrating a perception of艮as an unlucky direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=101|ISBN=4-582-76406-1}}</ref> In {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taiwan|qq=}}, Kimon is considered the "gateway between this world and the next," opening during the {{ill|Ghost Month|ja|鬼月|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ghost Month|qq=}} in the seventh lunar month.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれるLunisolar Julyの意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY|date=2016-08-12}}</ref>
== Reasons for Fearing Kimon ==
The term "Kimon" appears in the Eastern Han period's [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]]’s ''[[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]]'', in the ''Correcting Ghosts'' chapter, citing the ''[[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Classic of Mountains and Seas]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=28-29}}</ref>
{{Quotation|According to the ''Classic of Mountains and Seas,'' there is a Dousaku Mountain (度朔山) in the Eastern Sea. Atop the mountain stands a giant peach tree that spans 3,000 ri, curving around its branches. The area between the branches to the northeast is called Kimon, where myriad ghosts pass through. Two divine figures guard this place, binding malevolent ghosts with reed ropes to be fed to tigers. Consequently, the Yellow Emperor established rituals, erecting a large peachwood doll at the gate and hanging reed ropes to ward off evil spirits.|}}
In ancient China, the transition from winter to spring marked the year’s end, a period associated with ghosts causing diseases and calamities. Rituals were performed to drive out these spirits and welcome spring’s fortune. These practices, transmitted to Japan, evolved into seasonal events like [[:en:Setsubun|Setsubun]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=31-32}}</ref>
Kimon's association with demons also stems from its connection to {{ill|Onmyōdō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōdō|qq=}} practices that integrated with Japan's [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|pages=36-37}}</ref>
== Perceptions of Kimon (Authority) ==
Rulers established rituals like the Kyoto’s {{ill|Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|qq=}} to protect the city from disasters.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> For example, the monk [[:en:Jien|Jien]] described [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] as guarding Kyoto’s northeastern Kimon direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=128}}</ref>
== Popular Practices ==
Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

Kimon (northeast) is associated with "demon gate," while the southwest (Urakimon) is referred to as "people gate" or "illness gate," the southeast ({{ill|Sun|ja|巽|1=Xun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=巽|lt=Xun (巽)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sun|qq=}}) as "wind gate," and the northwest as "heaven gate" according to [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|author=小池康寿|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> In the [[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatari]], an [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]] named {{ill|Yuge no Koreo|ja|弓削是雄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuge no Koreo|qq=}} predicts an assassin's presence in the northeast direction of {{ill|Tomonokimi Yotsugi|ja|伴宿禰世継|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tomonokimi Yotsugi|qq=}}’s residence, illustrating a perception of艮as an unlucky direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=101|ISBN=4-582-76406-1}}</ref> In {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taiwan|qq=}}, Kimon is considered the "gateway between this world and the next," opening during the {{ill|Ghost Month|ja|鬼月|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ghost Month|qq=}} in the seventh lunar month.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれるLunisolar Julyの意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY|date=2016-08-12}}</ref>
== Reasons for Fearing Kimon ==
The term "Kimon" appears in the Eastern Han period's [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]]’s ''[[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]]'', in the ''Correcting Ghosts'' chapter, citing the ''[[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Classic of Mountains and Seas]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=28-29}}</ref>
{{Quotation|According to the ''Classic of Mountains and Seas,'' there is a Dousaku Mountain (度朔山) in the Eastern Sea. Atop the mountain stands a giant peach tree that spans 3,000 ri, curving around its branches. The area between the branches to the northeast is called Kimon, where myriad ghosts pass through. Two divine figures guard this place, binding malevolent ghosts with reed ropes to be fed to tigers. Consequently, the Yellow Emperor established rituals, erecting a large peachwood doll at the gate and hanging reed ropes to ward off evil spirits.|}}
In ancient China, the transition from winter to spring marked the year’s end, a period associated with ghosts causing diseases and calamities. Rituals were performed to drive out these spirits and welcome spring’s fortune. These practices, transmitted to Japan, evolved into seasonal events like [[:en:Setsubun|Setsubun]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=31-32}}</ref>
Kimon's association with demons also stems from its connection to {{ill|Onmyōdō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōdō|qq=}} practices that integrated with Japan's [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|pages=36-37}}</ref>
== Perceptions of Kimon (Authority) ==
Rulers established rituals like the Kyoto’s {{ill|Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō Shishū Ekijin Sai|qq=}} to protect the city from disasters.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> For example, the monk [[:en:Jien|Jien]] described [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] as guarding Kyoto’s northeastern Kimon direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=128}}</ref>
== Popular Practices ==
Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サル}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.

In Japan, this direction has traditionally been considered ominous and is associated with the entrance and exit of demons.
== Overview ==
The direction opposite to Kimon, the southwest ({{ill|Kon|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kon|qq=}}, {{ill|Hinoeuma|ja|未申|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoeuma|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 坤}}), is called '''Urakimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded as inauspicious. Kimon (northeast) is associated with "demon gate," while the southwest (Urakimon) is referred to as "people gate" or "illness gate," the southeast ({{ill|Sun|ja|巽|1=Xun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=巽|lt=Xun (巽)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sun|qq=}}) as "wind gate," and the northwest as "heaven gate" according to [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|author=小池康寿|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=37}}</ref> In the [[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatari]], an [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]] named {{ill|Yuge no Koreo|ja|弓削是雄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuge no Koreo|qq=}} predicts an assassin's presence in the northeast direction of {{ill|Tomonokimi Yotsugi|ja|伴宿禰世継|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tomonokimi Yotsugi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}’s residence, illustrating a perception of艮as an unlucky direction.<ref>{{Cite book|author=村山修一|title=日本陰陽道史話|publisher=平凡社|year=1988|page=101|ISBN=4-582-76406-1}}</ref> In {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taiwan|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}, Kimon is considered the "gateway between this world and the next," opening during the {{ill|Ghost Month|ja|鬼月|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ghost Month|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the seventh lunar month.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jp.taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=190&post=103467|title=「鬼月」と呼ばれるLunisolar Julyの意味|work=TAIWAN TODAY|date=2016-08-12}}</ref>

The term "Kimon" appears in the Eastern Han period's [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]]’s ''[[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]]'', in the ''Correcting Ghosts'' chapter, citing the ''[[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Classic of Mountains and Seas]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|author=水野杏紀|title=易、風水、暦、養生、処世 東アジアの宇宙観|publisher=講談社選書メチエ|year=2016|pages=28-29}}</ref>
{{Quotation|According to the ''Classic of Mountains and Seas,'' there is a Dousaku Mountain (度朔山) in the Eastern Sea. Atop the mountain stands a giant peach tree that spans 3,000 ri, curving around its branches. The area between the branches to the northeast is called Kimon, where myriad ghosts pass through. Consequently, the Yellow Emperor established rituals, erecting a large peachwood doll at the gate and hanging reed ropes to ward off evil spirits.|}}

Rituals were performed to drive out these spirits and welcome spring’s fortune. == Popular Practices ==
Traditionally, objects such as [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|Nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nandina|qq=}} were planted in northeast corners to repel misfortune. Kyoto’s [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Gosho]] features a recessed northeastern section known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugakuzuka]], believed to protect against Kimon.<ref>{{Cite book|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=プレジデント社|year=2015|page=28}}</ref>

'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サル}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.

'''Kimon''' (鬼門) refers to the {{ill|northeast|ja|北東|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/northeast|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} direction ({{ill|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|ja|艮|1=Gen (Bagua)|2=ja|3=艮|lt=Gen (艮)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/艮|qq=}}, representing the space between {{ill|Ox (zodiac)|ja|丑|1=Ox (Zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|1=Ox (zodiac)|lt=Ox (丑)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox (zodiac)|qq=}} and {{ill|Tiger (zodiac)|ja|寅|1=Tiger (Zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|2=ja|3=寅|1=Tiger (zodiac)|lt=Tiger (寅)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|13=User:Immanuelle/Tiger (zodiac)|qq=}}), considered an inauspicious direction in Japanese tradition, believed to be the gateway for malevolent spirits.
== Overview == The direction opposite to {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, the {{ill|southwest|ja|南西|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/southwest|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} ({{ill|Kun|ja|坤|1=Kun (Bagua)|2=ja|3=坤|lt=Kun (坤)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kun|qq=}}, representing {{ill|Goat (zodiac)|ja|未|1=Goat (Zodiac)|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat (zodiac)|qq=}} and [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]]), is known as the '''Ura-Kimon''' (裏鬼門) and is similarly regarded with apprehension. In [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]], the four corners are designated as gates: {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} in the northeast, {{ill|Fūmon|ja|風門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Chimon|ja|地門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chimon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the southeast, {{ill|Jinmon|ja|人門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Byōmon|ja|病門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in the southwest, and {{ill|Tenmon (direction)|ja|天門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon (direction)|qq=}} in the northwest.
== Reasons for Fear of Kimon == The term "{{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}" appears in ancient Chinese texts, such as the [[:en:Lunheng|Lunheng]] by [[:en:Wang Chong|Wang Chong]], referencing the [[:en:Classic of Mountains and Seas|Shan Hai Jing]]. It describes a large peach tree guarding the gate through which countless spirits pass. Although this passage isn't present in current versions of "Shan Hai Jing," it illustrates early beliefs associating the northeast with spirits.
== Interpretations by Rulers == In historical Japan, rulers performed rituals at the four corners of the capital to prevent misfortune. The [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] saw the rise of fear toward {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}, believed to cause calamities like disease, disasters, and curses. For example, [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] was considered to block the "demon gate" of {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}}.
== Popular Beliefs == Common folk also practiced protective measures against {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}}. In [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]], a carved monkey ({{ill|Saru|ja|猿|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saru|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サル}}) guards the northeast corner, known as [[:en:Sarugatsuji|Sarugatsuji]]. People planted [[:en:Osmanthus heterophyllus|holly]] and {{ill|nandina|ja|ナンテン|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nandina|qq=}} near their homes' northeastern corners to ward off evil.
== Denial of Kimon Beliefs == During the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], modernization labeled {{ill|Kimon|ja|鬼門|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimon|qq=}} beliefs as superstition. Scholars like [[:en:Mori Arinori|Arinori Mori]] criticized such practices, though traditional beliefs persisted among the public.
== References == * Seikei Kiyoshi, ''Modern House Fortunes'' (1989), ISBN 978-4106019678 * Yasuhisa Koike, ''The Correct Home Fortunes for Japanese People'' (2015), ISBN 978-4833421492
== See Also == * [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] * [[:en:Feng shui|Feng Shui]] * [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] * [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]]
